Visit note | 2025-11-26 10:00 AM | Dr. Towhid Alam, ENT | Patient: Saad Dewan, 29, male. Mr. Dewan attends for review regarding his ongoing symptoms, reporting a runny nose, frequent sneezing fits, and itchy eyes. He mentions that his symptoms have become much worse since keeping a cat at home in Banani. He works as a ride-share driver and is exposed to various outdoor allergens daily. He has Type 2 diabetes mellitus. He denies fever, facial pain, or breathing difficulties. On examination, he experiences about 12 sneezing fits a day. Other vitals: BP 123/79 mmHg, pulse 84 bpm, weight 48 kg. Nasal mucosa appears pale and boggy, but the throat is clear. Assessment: Allergic rhinitis. Plan: chronic follow-up; continue current medicines, no new prescription issued today. He was advised to avoid dust, wear a mask when cleaning, and wash bedding weekly. Follow-up in 1 month.

He lives with his family in Dhaka and has no reported history of chronic medical conditions such as diabetes or hypertension. He denies any history of substance abuse, head trauma, or chronic neurological disorders. During the mental state examination today, he is fully oriented to time, place, and person, though he appears visibly anxious and restless while describing his symptoms. His speech is coherent and of normal rate, and his mood is anxious with a congruent affect. He specifically denies experiencing any depressive thoughts, visual or auditory hallucinations, or thoughts of self-harm. Other clinical vitals recorded during the examination include a blood pressure of 133/71 mmHg, a pulse rate of 90 bpm, and a body weight of 87 kg. Cardiovascular examination reveals regular rhythm without murmurs, and respiratory examination is unremarkable. Based on the clinical history and evaluation, the assessment is Panic disorder. Regarding the management plan, chronic follow-up was advised to continue current medicines, and no new prescription was issued today. He was counselled in detail on lifestyle modifications, specifically advised to practise slow breathing during acute attacks, reduce dietary caffeine intake, and start structured psychotherapy or counselling sessions. Follow-up is scheduled in 4 weeks.
